```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)

# fill-in table drawn with base graphics; 'answer_cols' are drawn in magenta italic
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL, answer_cols = integer(0),
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5, cex = 0.95) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
    text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, h_total - header_height / 2, headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  }
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      is_ans <- j %in% answer_cols
      text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, y - row_height / 2, body[[i]][[j]], cex = cex,
           col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black", font = if (is_ans) 3 else 1)
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

nq <- function(lines, rows = 0, extra = 0) {
  if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) return("")
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf("\n\\needspace{%.2fin}\n", 0.23 * lines + 0.15 + 0.3 * rows + extra))
}

f2 <- function(v) formatC(round(v, 2) + 0, format = "f", digits = 2)
f1 <- function(v) formatC(round(v, 1) + 0, format = "f", digits = 1)

library(mvtnorm)
seedlings <- read.csv("../../data/PinyonSeedlings.csv")

# Part 1 (six seedlings)
six <- seedlings[c(1:3, 9:11), ]
X6 <- cbind(1, as.numeric(six$plot == "B"), six$moisture)
xb <- as.vector(X6 %*% c(2, 1.5, 0.5))
xtx <- t(X6) %*% X6
V2 <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), 2)
q_same <- as.numeric(t(c(1, 1)) %*% solve(V2) %*% c(1, 1))
q_opp <- as.numeric(t(c(1, -1)) %*% solve(V2) %*% c(1, -1))
C3 <- matrix(c(1, 0.9, -0.9, 0.9, 1, 0.9, -0.9, 0.9, 1), 3)
eig_c <- eigen(C3)$values

# Part 2 (all 24)
X <- model.matrix(~ plot + moisture, data = seedlings)
y <- seedlings$growth
beta_ne <- as.vector(solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% y))
fit_lm <- lm(growth ~ plot + moisture, data = seedlings)
r <- y - as.vector(X %*% beta_ne)
sigma_mle <- sqrt(mean(r^2))
ll_dnorm <- sum(dnorm(r, 0, sigma_mle, log = TRUE))
ll_mvn <- dmvnorm(r, rep(0, 24), sigma_mle^2 * diag(24), log = TRUE)
mvr_msg <- tryCatch({MASS::mvrnorm(1000, rep(0, 3), C3); "no error"},
                    error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))

# early finish: one sigma per plot
plot_id <- as.integer(factor(seedlings$plot))
nll_3sig <- function(p) -sum(dnorm(y, X %*% p[1:4], exp(p[5:7])[plot_id], log = TRUE))
fit_3sig <- optim(c(coef(fit_lm), log(c(1, 1, 1))), nll_3sig, method = "BFGS")
aic_1 <- AIC(fit_lm)
aic_3 <- 2 * fit_3sig$value + 2 * 7
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta sans-serif type; longer answers have a bar in the margin.}

## The scenario

A restoration crew planted pinyon pine seedlings in three burned plots
(A, B, and C) in a Great Basin woodland. A year later you measured each
seedling's height growth (cm) and the soil moisture (%) next to it: 8
seedlings per plot, 24 in all. The six seedlings below are the first
three in plots A and B.

```{r six-seedlings}
knitr::kable(six[, c("plot", "seedling", "moisture")], row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Plot", "Seedling", "Soil moisture (%)"), align = "ccc")
```

The crew's model is an ANCOVA: each plot has its own intercept, and all
plots share one slope for soil moisture,

$$\text{growth}_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma^2), \qquad
\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_B\,[\text{plot B}]_i + \beta_m\,\text{moisture}_i$$

where $[\text{plot B}]_i$ is 1 for a plot-B seedling and 0 otherwise.
(For the six seedlings there are only two plots.)

**How much does soil moisture matter, and what does this model assume
about seedlings that grow side by side in the same plot?**

Please keep laptops closed until the banner in Part 2. Part 1 and the
group check-in are pen and paper.

## Part 1: The model as matrices (individual, ~40 min)

**1a.** Write the model matrix $X$ for the six seedlings, with columns
for $\beta_0$, $\beta_B$, and $\beta_m$ in that order.

\ansbegin

$$X = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 8 \\ 1 & 0 & 10 \\ 1 & 0 & 12 \\ 1 & 1 & 9 \\ 1 & 1 & 11 \\ 1 & 1 & 13
\end{pmatrix}$$

\ansend

**1b.** Take $\boldsymbol\beta = (2,\ 1.5,\ 0.5)^T$. Compute
$X\boldsymbol\beta$, and say what each of the three numbers in
$\boldsymbol\beta$ means for a seedling.

\ansbegin

$X\boldsymbol\beta = (`r paste(xb, collapse = ",\\ ")`)^T$ cm.
$\beta_0 = 2$: expected growth of a plot-A seedling at 0% moisture (an
extrapolation). $\beta_B = 1.5$: a plot-B seedling grows 1.5 cm more
than a plot-A seedling at the same moisture. $\beta_m = 0.5$: each extra
1% of soil moisture adds 0.5 cm of growth, in either plot.

\ansend

**1c.** Compute $X^TX$. What does each entry on its diagonal count or
add up?

\ansbegin

$$X^TX = \begin{pmatrix}
`r xtx[1, 1]` & `r xtx[1, 2]` & `r xtx[1, 3]` \\
`r xtx[2, 1]` & `r xtx[2, 2]` & `r xtx[2, 3]` \\
`r xtx[3, 1]` & `r xtx[3, 2]` & `r xtx[3, 3]`
\end{pmatrix}$$

Diagonal: the number of seedlings (6), the number in plot B (3), and the
sum of squared moisture values (`r xtx[3, 3]`).

\ansend

**1d.** Suppose the six growth values are independent with
$\sigma = 0.5$ cm. Write the covariance matrix $V$, its inverse, and
its determinant. Then suppose plot B is more variable, with
$\sigma_B = 1$ cm (plot A stays at 0.5). Write the new $V$, and write
the quadratic form $\mathbf{r}^TV^{-1}\mathbf{r}$ for a residual vector
$\mathbf{r} = (r_1, \ldots, r_6)^T$ as a sum. How much does a plot-B
residual count compared with a plot-A residual of the same size?

\ansbegin

$V = 0.25\,I$ (6 $\times$ 6), $V^{-1} = 4\,I$, and
$|V| = 0.25^6 = 1/4096 \approx `r signif(0.25^6, 3)`$.

With $\sigma_B = 1$: $V = \text{diag}(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 1, 1, 1)$ and

$$\mathbf{r}^TV^{-1}\mathbf{r} = 4(r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2) + (r_4^2 + r_5^2 + r_6^2)$$

A plot-B residual counts one quarter as much as a plot-A residual of the
same size.

\ansend

**1e.** Two seedlings grow side by side in the same plot, and their
residuals have correlation 0.5 (each with variance 1):

$$V = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Find $|V|$ and $V^{-1}$. Compute $\mathbf{r}^TV^{-1}\mathbf{r}$ for
$\mathbf{r} = (1, 1)^T$ and for $\mathbf{r} = (1, -1)^T$, and compare
both with independence ($V = I$). Which pattern of residuals is more
surprising when the seedlings are correlated, and why does that make
sense?

\ansbegin

$|V| = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75$, and
$V^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{0.75}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -0.5 \\ -0.5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 4/3 & -2/3 \\ -2/3 & 4/3 \end{pmatrix}$.

$(1, 1)$: `r f2(q_same)`. $(1, -1)$: `r f2(q_opp)`. Under independence
both are 2.

Residuals of opposite sign are more surprising. Correlated seedlings
are expected to be high or low together, so two seedlings both growing
more than predicted is less unusual than one high and one low.

\ansend

**1f.** Three seedlings, three proposed correlations:

$$C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.9 & -0.9 \\ 0.9 & 1 & 0.9 \\ -0.9 & 0.9 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Could this be the correlation matrix of their growth? Explain without
computing anything.

\ansbegin

No. Seedlings 1 and 2 rise and fall together, and so do 2 and 3, so 1
and 3 must also be positively correlated; they can't be strongly
negatively correlated.

\ansend

## Part 2: Check it with R (laptop, ~50 min)

**Using AI:** each question has a recommendation. *Recommended: no AI*
marks the core skill of the lab (building and using model and
covariance matrices); R's help pages, web search, and classmates are
fine. *AI optional* marks work where the results matter but writing the
code by hand isn't the point. After each question, circle how you
actually used AI.

**What to turn in:** your filled-in answers. You don't need to submit
your code.

The data for all 24 seedlings are on the course website:

```{r data-url, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
data_url <-
  "https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/data/PinyonSeedlings.csv"
seedlings <- read.csv(data_url)
```

`r nq(9, 0, extra = 2.2)`

**2a.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Build $X$ for all 24 seedlings with
`model.matrix(~ plot + moisture, data = seedlings)`. Solve the normal
equations, $X^TX\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = X^T\mathbf{y}$, using `%*%`,
`t()`, and `solve()`, and check your answer against `lm()`. Check: the
moisture slope should be `r f2(coef(fit_lm)["moisture"])`. Fill in
the table.

```{r coef-table, fig.height=0.35 + 4 * 0.45}
nm <- c("(Intercept)", "plotB", "plotC", "moisture")
blank_table(c("Coefficient", "Normal equations", "lm()"),
            lapply(1:4, function(k) c(nm[k], f2(beta_ne[k]), f2(coef(fit_lm)[k]))),
            col_widths = c(1.4, 1.5, 1.2), answer_cols = 2:3, row_height = 0.45)
```

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

**2b.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* At your $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and the
MLE $\hat\sigma = \sqrt{\sum r_i^2 / n}$, compute the log-likelihood two
ways: with `sum(dnorm(..., log = TRUE))`, and with
`mvtnorm::dmvnorm(..., log = TRUE)` using $V = \hat\sigma^2 I$.

$\hat\sigma =$ \ans{`r f2(sigma_mle)`} cm. &nbsp;&nbsp; `sum(dnorm())`:
\ans{`r f2(ll_dnorm)`} &nbsp;&nbsp; `dmvnorm()`: \ans{`r f2(ll_mvn)`}

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

**2c.** *(AI optional.)* Check your answers to 1e and 1f with `det()`,
`solve()`, and `eigen()`. Then try to draw 1000 random values for three
seedlings from a multivariate normal with correlation matrix $C$ from
1f, using `MASS::mvrnorm()`. What happens? What do the eigenvalues of
$C$ tell you?

Eigenvalues of $C$: \ans{`r f1(eig_c[1])`}, \ans{`r f1(eig_c[2])`},
\ans{`r f1(eig_c[3])`}

\ansbegin

`mvrnorm()` stops with an error ("`r mvr_msg`"). One eigenvalue is
negative, so $C$ isn't positive definite: some weighted combination of
the three seedlings would have a negative variance.

\ansend

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

**2d.** Where did you use AI, if anywhere, and what did you have to
check or fix? If you didn't use it, what was hardest to get working?

\ans{Open-ended.}

## Group discussion and revision (~15 min)

Close laptops. Here is a different covariance matrix someone proposed
for the six seedlings in the table (rows and columns in the same
order: A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, B3):

$$V = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0.6 & 0.6 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0.6 & 1 & 0.6 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0.6 & 0.6 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0.6 & 0.6 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0.6 & 1 & 0.6 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0.6 & 0.6 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$$

With your group, say what this $V$ claims about the seedlings, and what
could make the 0.6s biologically reasonable. Should the crew treat its
24 seedlings as 24 independent replicates when reporting the effect of
plot? Record your answer, any changes you made to earlier answers, new
insights, and any "muddiest points" or topics you want to review.

\ansbegin

Each seedling has variance 1; seedlings in the same plot are correlated
(0.6) and seedlings in different plots are independent. Shared soil,
burn severity, microclimate, herbivores, or planting date could make
seedlings in a plot grow alike. If so, the 24 seedlings aren't 24
independent replicates of "plot": plot differences rest on three plots,
and treating seedlings as replicates overstates the evidence.

\ansend

**If you finish early.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Plot C's seedlings
look more scattered than the others. Write a negative log-likelihood
that gives each plot its own $\sigma$ (a diagonal $V$ with unequal
entries, as in 1d), fit it with `optim()`, and compare its AIC with the
one-$\sigma$ model.

$\hat\sigma_A =$ \ans{`r f2(exp(fit_3sig$par[5]))`} &nbsp;
$\hat\sigma_B =$ \ans{`r f2(exp(fit_3sig$par[6]))`} &nbsp;
$\hat\sigma_C =$ \ans{`r f2(exp(fit_3sig$par[7]))`}

AIC (one $\sigma$): \ans{`r f1(aic_1)`} &nbsp;&nbsp; AIC (three):
\ans{`r f1(aic_3)`}
